newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Easing still on agenda in spite of RBNZ - economists.
newsitem.headline: Easing still on agenda in spite of RBNZ - economists.

text.p: New Zealand economists on Friday snubbed the Reserve Bank's call to take an easing in monetary conditions off the economic agenda, saying interest rates could fall even before the end of the year.
In its six-monthly Economic Projections, the central bank said despite "quite encouraging" medium-term prospects, too much uncertainty surrounded the short-term inflation outlook.

"An easing remains off the agenda until conclusive evidence is at hand that inflation will in fact fall away sharply next year and beyond," Reserve Bank Governor Don Brash said. The bank's interest and exchange rate assumptions implied slightly firmer monetary conditions until late 1997, easing slightly thereafter.
But economists said an easing was still very much on the agenda for the financial markets, which had expected the bank to ease by early 1997.
"It's just a case of holding the line in the near term and we still think an easing in policy in early '97, possibly late '96, is still likely," said ANZ chief economist Paul Stewart.
"We still think that if pressures continue to moderate, particularly in the housing market, then there will be some scope for falls in interest rates throughout 1997."
The bank forecast annual underlying inflation to peak at 2.7 percent in the September 1996 quarter before falling to 2.1 percent in the March 1997 year, 0.8 percent in 1998 and 0.5 percent in 1999.
Westpac chief economist Bevan Graham agreed there was too much uncertainty on the inflation front for the bank to sanction an easing at this stage.
"Having said that, though, I think that there are still some pretty good signs out there from an inflation perspective."

He said declining business and consumer confidence levels, a weaker growth outlook and early signs that the labour market was weakening suggested there was room for an easing earlier than the Reserve Bank's projection.
"Definitely we can't rule out an earlier easing," he said, adding that a lot would depend on how the next round of partial indicators panned out.
"If that data remains reasonably robust...then increasingly we would start pushing out that expectation of an easing."

Brash warned that the bank would "resist vigorously" any significant easing in overall conditions relative to those assumed in its projections, but BNZ economist Tony Alexander said he expected the market to ease earlier than the bank wished anyway.

"The poor old Reserve Bank these days has to some extent limited control of monetary conditions," he said. "Your average house buyer and residential investor is going to be using fixed interest rates and not floating rates, and that's not what the Reserve Bank can influence.
"So I think the market will be driving an easing in monetary conditions which the Reserve Bank will probably not be able to prevent," he said.
"They'll be doing their thing with the short end of the curve but the long end of the curve where everyone is borrowing will be doing something totally different."

Economists said the bank's assumption of a flat New Zealand dollar Trade-Weighted Index at 65.0 was the bank's way of validating the market-driven tightening which had taken place over the last quarter.
The TWI is currently above 66.
"So monetary conditions are yet again tighter than they (the RBNZ) have assumed," Graham said.
"At some point there's going to be some adjustment either in the exchange rate downward or interest rates re going to be driven downward by the firm exchange rate," he said.
--Wellington Newsroom (64 4) 4734746
